court: Supreme Court, Appellate Term, First Department
holding_summary: In a summary holdover proceeding against a tenant conducting a rooming house, the landlord was entitled to a directed verdict for possession of the ten rooms occupied by the tenant's roomers, since the tenant's peaceful occupation of her own seven rooms would not be seriously affected by putting the roomers' rooms in another's possession. The trial court erred in submitting the question to a jury because all the physical facts were undisputed.

quotes.text: the landlord merely sought the possession of those parts of the premises occupied by the roomers, since the tenant’s reasonable and peaceful occupation of her rooms would not be seriously interfered with if the landlord obtained possession, and whatever detriment would result from the ouster would be to the landlord or the roomers rather than to the tenant.
It seems to us that whatever detriment would result from the ouster would be one to the landlord or the roomers, not to the tenant, and the landlord’s motion should have been granted.

notes: Court never expressly characterizes the roomers' legal relation (lease/license/lodging); it resolves only the landlord's priority in possession over a holdover tenant's sub-occupants, treating the roomers as lacking an independently protectable interest -- left characterization null for lack of a supporting quote.

holding_summary: Where a householder let a room with board to occupants, first for a stated one-month term and then under a converted arrangement paying weekly at four-week intervals continuing indefinitely at the landlord's option, the arrangement was an indefinite tenancy analogous to a tenancy at will, requiring thirty days' notice under Real Property Law section 228. Because the notice given was untimely, the dispossession petition was properly dismissed, and the court did not need to decide whether the parties stood as landlord and tenant or as boarding-house keeper and boarders.

quotes.text: But under the new agreement as set forth in the petition, the defendants were four-weekly tenants for an indefinite period, that is to say, from four weeks to four weeks, analogous to month to month, at the option of the landlord.

But under the new agreement as set forth in the petition, the defendants were four-weekly tenants for an indefinite period, that is to say, from four weeks to four weeks, analogous to month to month, at the option of the landlord.

Having disposed of the case on that ground it is not necessary to consider whether the agreement set forth in the petition constituted the parties as landlord and tenant or mere boarding house keeper and boarders.

notes: Court expressly declines to decide whether the relation was landlord-tenant or boarding-house-keeper/boarder, resolving the case solely on the notice requirement; characterization left null because no quote resolves it either way.
